steps.do: Install Textual and the async test plugin.
Create the Save button with disabled set to True so it starts inactive.
In on_input_changed, set the button disabled flag to not event.value.strip().
Run the test that leaves the input empty and checks the button is disabled.

K-020983.example: Create Button('Save', id='save', disabled=True) in compose, then set self.query_one('#save', Button).disabled = not event.value.strip() in on_input_changed. Typing 'a' enables the button and deleting it back to spaces disables it again.
K-020983.check: pytest -q prints '1 passed', and the test asserts button.disabled is True when the input is empty.
traps: Small models often skip strip(), so a value of only spaces enables the button.
Setting the flag on a Static or Label does nothing to the real Button, which stays clickable.
Async tests fail with 'async def functions are not natively supported' when pytest-asyncio is missing.

steps.do: Find the press handler that calls the save function.
Wrap the save call in try, and on OSError set event.button.variant to 'error' and event.button.label to 'Retry'.
On success set variant back to 'default' and label back to 'Save' so the red state does not stick.
Run the test that forces save to raise OSError and checks the variant.
Run the full test folder to confirm no older test broke.

K-020984.example: A save that raises OSError turns the Save button red and relabels it 'Retry'. A later successful save returns it to 'default' with the label 'Save'.
K-020984.check: pytest -q prints 'N passed' with no 'failed' text, and the error test asserts button.variant == 'error'.
traps: Textual's valid variant name is 'error', not 'danger' or 'red', and an invalid name raises an error.
Forgetting to reset variant on success leaves the button red after recovery.
Catching the exception in a worker instead of the press handler means the button never changes.

steps.do: List the buttons in the app so you can find the delete button.
Set the Delete button disabled to True when the items list length is 0, and False otherwise.
When the list is empty, set the button label to 'No items', which is 8 characters.
Run the test that starts with items equal to an empty list.

K-020985.example: With items=[] the button reads 'No items' and disabled is True. Adding one item sets the label back to 'Delete' and disabled to False.
K-020985.check: pytest -q prints '1 passed', and the test asserts len(button.label) is 8 or less and button.disabled is True.
traps: Small models often update the label but forget to set disabled, so the empty button still fires.
Checking the list before it loads can show the empty state for a moment; check after the first refresh.
Hard-coding the count as a string instead of comparing len(items) to 0 breaks when items change.

steps.do: Confirm the installed Textual version supports widget tooltips.
Find existing tooltip uses in the project.
On TimeoutError set button.variant to 'error' and button.tooltip to 'Network timeout. Retry in 5s.', which is 32 characters.
Run the test that simulates a timeout and checks the tooltip text.

K-020986.example: A TimeoutError sets the Retry button tooltip to 'Network timeout. Retry in 5s.' (32 characters) and leaves disabled False. The test asserts the tooltip string and that the button can still be pressed.
K-020986.check: pytest -q prints '1 passed', and the test asserts button.tooltip equals the expected 32-character string.
traps: Tooltip needs a Textual release with widget tooltips, so pip show textual should report a recent version.
Disabling the button to show the error blocks the retry the message promises.
Long tooltip text can exceed the screen width, so keep it under 60 characters.

Check that the nav link tap target is at least 44px tall, and note the line that sets it.

traps: Small models often count hex values but skip named colors like white.
Do not invent tokens for roles the nav does not use.
Do not delete existing colors before the plan lists them.

steps.do: Decide that :root holds the light values and html[data-theme='dark'] overrides only the changed tokens.
Write the planned token names, each starting with --nav-, to the terminal for review.
Confirm index.html exists, since the data-theme attribute goes on its html element.
Count data-theme attributes in index.html, which should be 0 before the build stage.
Check that the Playwright runner is installed so theme and contrast tests can run later.

K-020990.example: Set --nav-bg: #ffffff in :root and --nav-bg: #14141f under html[data-theme='dark']. Only the five changed tokens appear in the dark block, so the file stays short. The version check confirms the runner exists before the 4.5:1 contrast test is written.
K-020990.check: ls prints index.html, the echo lists six token names, grep prints 0 which confirms the plan starts from no theme attribute, and npx prints a Playwright version number.
traps: Small models often repeat every token in the dark block, which doubles maintenance.
Do not put theme selectors on the nav element, since the attribute belongs on html.
Do not use a class name when the plan says data-theme.

steps.do: Plan three stored values, light, dark, and system, with system as the default.
Search for an existing prefers-color-scheme rule to decide whether to reuse it.
Plan the storage key as theme in localStorage and read it before first paint.
Check whether color-scheme is already declared in the tokens file.
Check that the Playwright runner is installed so the 200ms theme-switch test can run later.

K-020991.example: A user with OS dark mode and no stored choice sees the dark nav. Picking light in the menu saves light under localStorage key theme, and picking system removes the key so the OS rule applies again. The version check confirms the runner is ready for the switch-timing test.
K-020991.check: On a fresh project both grep commands print nothing, so the plan must add a prefers-color-scheme block and the three stored values, and npx prints a Playwright version number.
traps: Small models often store system as a literal dark value, which freezes the OS setting.
Do not read localStorage after the page paints, which causes a flash.
Do not skip color-scheme on :root, since native scrollbars and form controls stay light otherwise.

Confirm the page has a nav element to target with its theme rules.

K-020992.check: The echo prints five state names, grep for the nav element prints at least one line number, the transition count gives the number of overrides to plan, and the duration grep prints each value with its line so it can be compared against 200ms.

Do not treat forced-colors as the same thing as dark mode.

steps.do: Create the app file btn_tui/app.py.
Define a constant NARROW_WIDTH equal to 60 at the top of app.py.
Add an on_resize method to ButtonApp that adds the class narrow to the Container with id buttons when self.size.width is below NARROW_WIDTH, and removes it otherwise.
In app.tcss, set #buttons to layout horizontal and #buttons.narrow to layout vertical.
Confirm the on_resize method is defined in app.py.
Run the narrow-layout test and confirm it passes.

K-020993.example: At 50 columns, the handler adds narrow to #buttons, so the three buttons stack vertically. At 80 columns it removes the class, and the buttons return to one horizontal row.
K-020993.check: grep prints a line number for on_resize, and pytest prints '1 passed' with exit code 0.
traps: Reading self.size in on_mount can return zero before the first layout, so use on_resize for width changes. Adding narrow without removing it at wide sizes leaves the buttons stacked.
Hardcoding 60 in several places makes the breakpoints drift apart, so keep one NARROW_WIDTH constant.

steps.do: Create btn_tui/labels.py to hold the fit_label helper.
Define fit_label(text, width) to return text unchanged when len(text) is at most width minus 4 cells.
When the text is longer, return the first width minus 5 characters followed by a single one-cell ellipsis character.
Import fit_label in app.py and call it on each Button label inside on_resize.
Find every use of fit_label to confirm it is wired in.
Run the label tests and confirm they pass.

K-020994.check: pytest prints 'N passed' with no failures, and rg lists at least two lines: the definition and the call in app.py.

steps.do: Change into the fm-chart-motion crate directory.
Create src/motion.rs with a Tween struct holding from, to, start as Instant, and duration as Duration.
Implement value(now) using elapsed seconds divided by duration seconds, clamped to 0.0 through 1.0, then smoothstep t times t times (3 minus 2 times t).
Add mod motion; near the top of src/main.rs so the module compiles.
Add a #[cfg(test)] module asserting that a tween from 50.0 to 100.0 over 200ms returns 75.0 at 100ms.
Run only the motion tests.
Check formatting of the new file.

K-020997.example: A y-axis tween from [0.0, 50.0] to [0.0, 100.0] over 200ms reaches 75.0 at the halfway point. Each frame calls value with Instant::now, so speed does not depend on the frame rate.
K-020997.check: cargo test motion prints 'test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed' or more with 0 failed.
traps: Small models often advance the tween by one step per frame, which makes the speed depend on frame rate; use elapsed time from Instant.
Skipping the clamp lets t exceed 1.0 and the bounds overshoot the target.
Comparing floats with == at the end of a tween can fail by rounding; compare within 1e-9.

steps.do: Change into the fm-chart-motion crate directory.
Create src/window.rs with a SampleWindow holding a VecDeque of (f64, f64) pairs and a capacity of 120.
Implement push so it appends the sample with an absolute index as x and pops the front when the length exceeds 120.
Add a test that pushes 130 samples and asserts the length is 120 and the first x is 10.0.
Run the window tests.

K-020998.example: After 130 pushes the window holds indexes 10 through 129, so the x-axis bounds become [10.0, 129.0]. The x values are absolute, so the line slides instead of restarting at zero.
K-020998.check: cargo test window prints 'test result: ok' with the new test listed as passed and 0 failed.
traps: Small models often reset x to zero each frame, which makes the line jump back to the left edge.
Forgetting to pop the front lets memory grow without limit during a long stream.
When the window holds one sample the x bounds have min equal to max, which Ratatui cannot draw; pad the bounds by 1.0.

steps.do: Change into the fm-chart-motion crate directory.
Add a Motion enum with On and Off variants in src/motion.rs.
Add a duration method that returns Duration::ZERO for Off and the base duration for On.
In src/main.rs, read std::env::args and select Motion::Off when the argument --reduce-motion is present.
Add a test asserting that Motion::Off returns Duration::ZERO for a 200ms base.
Run the reduced-motion test.

K-020999.example: Running the binary with --reduce-motion gives every tween a duration of zero, so the chart jumps straight to the target bounds. The default run keeps the 200ms tween.
K-020999.check: cargo test reduced_motion prints 'test result: ok' with 1 passed and 0 failed.
traps: Small models often divide by a zero duration in the easing code, which produces NaN; return the target value directly when the duration is zero.
Reading the flag after the loop starts means the first frames still animate.

steps.do: Change into the fm-chart-motion crate directory.
Create tests/frame_budget.rs that builds a Terminal over ratatui::backend::TestBackend at 120 columns by 40 rows.
In the test, draw the chart 300 times and assert that the average time per draw is below 16ms.
Run the test in release mode with output shown.

K-021000.example: The test draws a 200-sample chart 300 times at 120 by 40 and prints the average draw time. The assert fails when the average is 16ms or more.
K-021000.check: cargo test --release frame_budget prints 'test frame_budget ... ok' and the printed average is below 16ms.
traps: Small models often run the frame test in debug mode, which gives timings that do not match the shipped build; always pass --release.
TestBackend skips terminal write cost, so a passing draw time does not prove the real terminal keeps up.

steps.do: List frame width values from 0 to 99 in Swift files, which catches small controls.
Count the 44pt minimum frames already in the nav code.
Write each undersized control into the plan with a fix that sets a minimum 44 by 44 pt frame.

K-021001.example: rg finds a frame(width: 28) on the toolbar close button in NavBar.swift, so the plan adds .frame(minWidth: 44, minHeight: 44) and .contentShape(Rectangle()) to it. The count command then reports 1 existing 44pt frame.
K-021001.check: After the plan is written, the rg frame search lists only controls that the plan marks as fixed.
traps: Visible icon size is not the tap target; the frame and contentShape define the hit area.
The 44 figure is in points (pt), not pixels, so do not convert it to 88px.
A frame(width: 60) match is not a problem, so only plan changes for values below 44.
